2. The facts of the cases, in short, are that Amulya Gopal Datta predecessor of the present respondents, as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No.225 of 1970 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong seeking declaration of two orders as void and illegal and for permanent injunction in respect of a small apartment consisting one bed room and a kitchen on the first floor, situated under Chittagong Municipal Holding No.812. The plaintiff claimed that he was a tenant under the landlord-Dhirendra Nath Sen at monthly rent of taka 35/- and subsequently, the rent was increased to taka 40/-. The landlord realized rent from him, but the receipts were destroyed during the liberation war. Defendant No.4 took rent in respect of three rooms in the ground floor and other four rooms are in possession of other tenants. While the plaintiff was in possession, the landlord-Dhirendra Nath Sen wanted to evict him as a result, be did not repair the apartment. Accordingly, the plaintiff instituted House Rent Control Case No.1735 of 1966 for permission to repair the apartment. He also instituted another case for depositing rent and he was depositing rents in Court with the Rent Controller. The plaintiff also paid municipal taxes, After the death of Dhirendra Nath Sen in 1967, the property was enlisted as enemy property. Thereafter, the plaintiff prayed for lease from the Government in respect of the said two rooms apartment, but the Government served a notice upon him to vacate possession. Subsequently, the Government served a notice for payment of rent, but the Government instead of leasing out two-room illegally leased out the house to defendant No.4. The plaintiff claimed that the notices of the Government were illegal and without jurisdiction and also prayed for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from dispossessing him otherwise than in accordance with law. Subsequently, on the death of the original plaintiff, his heirs, the present respondent; were substituted in his place in the suit. 

 "The High Court Division misconceived the law and failed to consider that a lessee under Vested Property has no vested right to hold over and granting a decree for permanent injunction in favour of lessee against the Government is a mistake of law occasioning failure justice. 

 The Government having acquired right to dispose of enemy property by transfer or otherwise under Ordinance No.93 of 1976, the plaintiff cannot challenge the order of the Government leasing out the suit property in favour of the petitioner and that the High Court Division failed to notice that section 33 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 has excluded the application of the Act in case of premises of the Government and as such, the plaintiff cannot get a decree of permanent injunction in respect of a Government premises." 

 8. Mr. Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant in Civil Appeal ,No.588 of 2009, submits that the High Court Division misconceived the. law and failed to consider that a lessee has no vested right to hold over and granting a decree for permanent injunction in his favour against the Government in respect of the Government property and such view is a mistake of law occasioning failure justice. He further submits that the High Court Division did not appreciate that there is no office of Assistant Custodian and by reason of law, all vested properties have vested in the Government and the Government is competent authority to deal with such property. He further submits that the High Court Division committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in passing a decree for permanent injunction for indefinite period at the instance of a lessee against the Government. He lastly submits that the high Court Division upon conjecture and surmise and also on the basis of some spurious papers reversed the concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiffs are not entitled to maintain his possession since there was no lessee under the vested property authority holding that the Courts below thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 12. From the record, it appears that the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration that the order passed on 20.08.1970 in V.P. Miscellaneous Case Nos.427/67-68 and 467/67-68 is void, illegal in operative and without jurisdiction and also for an order of permanent injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the suit land wherein the plaintiff claimed to be a bharaita (lessee). 

 reside in a room situated at the first floor. It is also evident that landlord, Dhirendra Nath Sen died in the year, 1967 and his legal heirs left for India and used to reside there permanently. Accordingly, the suit premises has been enlisted as vested property. For the sake of argument, if we consider for a moment that all the plaintiffs were the monthly bharatia under landlord, Dhirendra Nath Sen in that case, tenancy right of the plaintiffs have been terminated soon after demise of landlord, Dhirendra Nath Sen. In the meantime, though Shibsankar Mitra died, but his heirs are residing in 4(four) rooms situated on the ground floor. Neither Amulya Gopal Datta nor the other heirs of Shibsankar Mitra had/have any status of monthly bharatia under the landlord, Dhirendra Nath Sen. When a property is enlisted as enemy property and vests upon the Government, there is no chance to hold over a tenancy under the vested property authority since lease of such property is renewable on year to year basis. 

 15. The High Court Division found that the learned Subordinate Judge in course of hearing noticed exhibits 2, 3, 5 series and 8 and found that those are related to the suit premises which the Government did not dispute at any stage of the proceedings. But the trial Court observed that 'PW3 failed to prove that he was a tenant of the suit premises since 1948, as if the learned Assistant Judge were deciding whether or not PW3 was a tenant under Dhirendra Nath Sen.' It has been further observed that 'all the three witnesses examined by the plaintiffs in unequivocal terms stated that the plaintiffs father was tenant under admitted owner and that exhibits 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 series corroborated his claim and those documentary evidence also proved that the plaintiffs' predecessor had instituted two cases against the landlord in respect of the suit premises.' It is also observed that 'House Rent Controller allowed the cases and also that the plaintiffs had been possessing in two rooms of the suit property from the time of their predecessor as tenants under admitted owner Dhirendra Nath Sen and thus, they could not be said to be trespassers in the suit premises.' 

 16. But the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellant cited a decision enunciated in the case of Farid Miah-Vs-Kutub Uddin reported in 46DLR(AD) 183 wherein it has been held that under section 4 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 the lessee is not entitled to hold over after expiry of the period of lease. It has been further held that: "Be that as it may, that period of lease of the plaintiff having already expired with the expiry of 1379 BS and there being no fresh settlement order in his favour, the plaintiff has no subsisting interest to maintain the suit. It has been noticed that under section 4 of the aforesaid Order, the plaintiff was not entitled to hold over after the expiry of the period of lease." 

 17. In the instant case, we find no scope for the plaintiff to retain possession since the vested property authority already leased out the property elsewhere when the plaintiffs did not accept the settlement made in their favour on their prayer. 

 18. On perusal of the entire evidence on record, it appears that the plaintiff-respondents are in possession of certain rooms of the suit premises, but they are unauthorized and undesirable occupants since the vested property authority has already leased out the same to defendant No.4 as its yearly lessee vide VP Miscellaneous Case No.427/67-68. Thus, the plaintiffs are unauthorized occupants and their possession cannot be protected by an order of injunction, as has been granted by the learned Single Judge of the, High Court Division vide the impugned judgment. Moreover, the Court cannot issue any direction to the vested property authority for leasing out the same in favour of the plaintiffs since it is the absolute domain of the vested property authority. Nor the plaintiff has come forward to seek relief in the mandatory form. 

 19. The plaintiffs have come with an allegation that the order dated 20.08.1970 and 04.08.1973 in respect of lease accorded in favour of defendant No.4 in VP Miscellaneous Case Nos.427/67-68 and 464/67-68 are declared, to be illegal, inoperative, and not binding upon them, but the trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal refused to grant such relief since the plaintiffs have no locus standi to challenge the aforementioned order as they have no right, title or tenancy right on the same. The facts, circumstances and materials on record lead us to hold that the aforementioned concurrent finding is sustainable in the premises of the case and as well as in the eye of law. But the High Court Division found that 'since the plain-tiffs have been possessing the suit premises as tenant under the admitted owner, they have prima facie right to remain in possession and therefore, they are legally entitled to maintain a suit for permanent injunction if their possession is threatened by anybody else.' It also held that 'the Court may incidentally enquire into the respective claims of the parties to such a suit for determining whether the plaintiff is entitled to specific relief for permanent injunction but the learned Assistant Judge committed error of law in dismissing the suit for permanent injunction and as such, this Rule succeeds in part.' 

 21. A person claiming possessory right is entitled to maintain his possession as against anybody else except the true owner. But in the instant case, the plaintiffs sought for relief against their true owner claiming themselves as ejectable monthly bharatia who has no legal right or character and they are admittedly defaulters in payment of rent. We have already found that there is no landlord tenant relationship in between the parties. Not only that the plaintiff is not entitled to hold over after the end of their leasing year. Over and above, the plaintiffs have no locus standi to file any suit since there is no year to year lessee even. 

 22. In view of the evidence that has been led in the case, both the trial Court and the Appellate Court after due consideration of the materials on record came to concurrent findings that the plaintiff-appellant failed to establish the existence of the landlord and tenant relationship in between them since there is neither any positive evidence to such fact nor there is any allegation of the, case of holding over after demise of landlord, Dhirendra Nath Scan and Shibsankar Mitra, the predecessor of the plaintiff. Thus, the revisional Court acted beyond its jurisdiction in setting aside the concurrent finding of fact and there is misreading and misappreciation of the evidence on record regarding fact of the case. Consequently, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and thereby the concurrent finding and decision of the two Courts below are restored.
